agentCan: Build the authorize redirect, code exchange, refresh loop (storing each new refresh token), and revocation calls
Implement the mandatory token validation: call /validate at app start and hourly thereafter

approval.cost: Not stated (no fee appears on any page read)
approval.trigger: No app review or approval process for standard API apps is stated on any page read (Authentication overview, Register Your App, Getting/Refreshing/Validating Tokens, Scopes): no review requirement, no timeline, no fee, no listing/marketplace process, and no user cap is stated. What exists instead is runtime enforcement: 'Twitch periodically conducts audits to discover applications that are not validating access tokens hourly as required. If your app shows up in an audit, Twitch will reach out to you to resolve the issue. If the issue is not resolved, Twitch reserves the right to take punitive action, such as revoking the developer's API key or throttling the application's performance.' The only numeric cap stated is token-related: 'the maximum number of valid access tokens that a refresh token can be associated with is 50' (creating the 51st fails).
approval.wait: None (no review exists in the pages read)

blockers.detail: 'Any third-party app that calls the Twitch APIs and maintains an OAuth session must call the /validate endpoint to verify that the access token is still valid... Your app must validate the OAuth token when it starts and on an hourly basis thereafter.' Twitch audits for this and can revoke the developer's API key or throttle the app. Valid = HTTP 200 (with client_id, scopes, expires_in, login, user_id); invalid = HTTP 401 'invalid access token'.
blockers.howToClear: Build validation into the session lifecycle from day one: at start, then hourly, and react to 401s by refreshing rather than trusting expires_in.
blockers.title: Hourly token validation is mandatory and audited

blockers.detail: 'You must copy the secret and store it somewhere safe. Getting a new secret invalidates the previous secret.' Rotation is a hard cutover with no overlap window documented.
blockers.howToClear: Rotate during a maintenance window and deploy the new secret atomically.
blockers.title: New secret invalidates the previous one

blockers.detail: Refresh behavior splits by client type: 'Most refresh tokens do not expire, but refresh tokens generated by a Public client type will expire 30 days after they are generated' (Confidential refresh tokens 'do not have an expiration time'), and device-flow public refresh tokens are 'one time use only'. Refresh tokens must also be URL-encoded when posted, or the request may fail with 'Invalid refresh token'. Only user access tokens created using the Authorization Code Grant Flow can be refreshed without new consent.
blockers.howToClear: Use a Confidential client for server apps, persist the new refresh token returned by every refresh, and URL-encode it.
blockers.title: Public-client refresh tokens expire in 30 days

alternatives: Implicit grant flow (user token; 'if your app does not use a server', e.g. client-side JavaScript or mobile apps)

Client credentials grant flow (app access token only, server-to-server, 'meant for apps that only need an app access token'; app access tokens don't use scopes and 'You cannot refresh app access tokens', you mint a new one)

Device code grant flow (user token for clients 'with limited input capabilities, such as set-top boxes or video games'; the only flow documented with public client types: public clients need no client secret and can refresh without one, but are limited to the device flow; device access tokens expire in 4 hours, the device code response example shows expires_in 1800 with interval 5 polling, and public device refresh tokens are one-time use with a 30-day expiry)
OIDC variants of the implicit and authorization-code flows (tabulated on the overview; additionally return an ID token)
flavor.recommended: The Authorization Code Grant Flow on a registered application (Confidential client)
flavor.why: The object is an 'application' (app) registered in the Twitch developer console (Applications tab): 'The first step to getting an access token is to register your application (this includes Twitch Extensions and chatbots).' Registration yields a Client ID ('Note your Client ID, which you'll use to get your access token and to set the Client-Id header in all API requests. Client IDs are considered public and can be embedded in a web page's source') and, for flows that need it, a client secret generated via 'New Secret'. For a third-party web service whose users connect their own accounts, the docs prescribe the authorization code grant flow: 'Use this flow if your app uses a server, can securely store a client secret, and can make server-to-server requests to the Twitch API.' It returns a user access token plus a refresh token. 'Most applications are set to the Confidential client type', and client_secret 'is not required if your application's client type was set to public'.

humanMust: Log in to the developer console with a Twitch account (create one via Sign Up if needed), verify the account via the email Twitch sends, and enable two-factor authentication (2FA) on the account (Security and Privacy), then refresh the console

Applications tab > Register Your Application: set a Name (must be unique among all Twitch applications), set OAuth Redirect URLs to your callback URL and click Add, select a Category, click the 'I'm not a robot' checkbox, click Create
Back in the Applications tab, open the app under Developer Applications > Manage; note the Client ID; if the flow requires it, click New Secret, copy the secret and store it safely
name: Twitch
nuances: 'Do not share client IDs among applications; each application must have its own client ID. Sharing client IDs among applications may result in the suspension of your application's access to the Twitch API.' Tokens and secrets should be treated 'like a password'.

Scopes: the scope list is space-delimited and must be URL-encoded, and 'An application must request only the scopes required by the APIs that their app calls. If you request more scopes than is required... Twitch may suspend your application's access.' The state parameter is optional but 'strongly encouraged' for CSRF (randomly generated, unique per request); force_verify defaults to false.

Token invalidation causes (overview): the token expires, the user changes their password, Twitch revokes it, or the user disconnects the app at /settings/connections > Disconnect. Revocation endpoint: POST id.twitch.tv/oauth2/revoke with client_id + token returns 200 OK with no body (400 'Invalid token', 404 'client does not exist').

Worked-example expires_in values (examples, not guarantees): authorization-code flow 14124 and 15485 seconds (about 4 hours); refresh examples 15583 and 5215742; validate example 5520838; client-credentials examples 5011271 (about 58 days).
prerequisites: A Twitch account with 2FA enabled for the developer console
A unique application name (unique among all Twitch applications)
A callback URL to register as the OAuth Redirect URL

steps.detail: Log in to the developer console (Twitch account, email verification, 2FA enabled). Applications tab > Register Your Application: Name (unique among all Twitch applications), OAuth Redirect URLs (your callback URL, click Add), Category, 'I'm not a robot' checkbox, Create. Then Manage the app: note the Client ID and, if needed, click New Secret and store the secret safely.
steps.title: Register the application in the developer console

steps.detail: Send the user to id.twitch.tv/oauth2/authorize (response_type=code, client_id, redirect_uri = your registered URI, scope space-delimited and URL-encoded, state strongly encouraged). POST the returned code to id.twitch.tv/oauth2/token with grant_type=authorization_code and your client_secret to get a user access token + refresh token. Send the Client-Id header on all API requests.
steps.title: Run the authorization code flow

steps.detail: At app start and hourly thereafter, GET id.twitch.tv/oauth2/validate with Authorization: OAuth <token> (Bearer also allowed). On 401, refresh: POST id.twitch.tv/oauth2/token with grant_type=refresh_token (URL-encode the refresh token), and safely store the NEW refresh token returned, since refresh tokens may change.
steps.title: Validate hourly; refresh on 401

steps.detail: POST id.twitch.tv/oauth2/revoke with client_id + token when a user disconnects (200 OK, no body).
steps.title: Revoke on disconnect

tagline: Self-service registration with no app review at all: the one real obligation is operational. Twitch requires you to validate every session token at startup and hourly after that, audits for it, and can revoke your API key if you do not.

time.active: ~10 min of console setup + ~1 hr of flow code
